---
title: "Deciding what counts as a word"
subtitle: "Compare word, sentence, and subword tokenization"
description: "Learn why tokenization is a rule-based decision before any word count can begin."
categories: [word parsing, tokenization, workforce research]
---

A planning meeting begins with the Lab's labeled sentences on the table. The
team has 28 reviewed text units from a job board page and a training flyer.
Six came from the flyer, and 22 came from job-detail lines.

The labels describe what each text unit says.
Before counting words, the Lab must also state what counts as a word.

::: {.callout-note}
The author created the fictional Riverton Workforce Lab, its job board, and
its training flyer for teaching.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## What you will learn

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

- explain how a rule creates tokens.
- compare whitespace and package word tokenizers.
- compare row counts before and after sentence tokenization.
- train a subword model without writing files into the project folder.
- explain which settings control the number of pieces in tokenized text.
:::

```{r}
#| include: false

options(warn = 2)
stopifnot(identical(getOption("warn"), 2L))
```

## Start with the sentence on the page

The first chunk loads readr for files and dplyr and tibble for tables.
It loads purrr for successive checks and stringr for strings.
The tokenizers package splits words and sentences, while tokenizers.bpe splits
subwords. A **tibble** is a tidyverse table that prints its dimensions and
each column's type.

```{r}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)
library(purrr)
library(stringr)
library(tokenizers)
library(tokenizers.bpe)

sentences <- read_csv(
  "data/workforce/workforce_sentences.csv",
  na = character(),
  col_types = cols(
    sentence_id = col_character(),
    document_id = col_character(),
    source_line = col_character(),
    text = col_character(),
    reference_label = col_character(),
    uncertainty = col_character(),
    annotator_id = col_character(),
    rationale = col_character(),
    codebook_version = col_character(),
    codebook_hash = col_character(),
    derived = col_character(),
    transformation = col_character()
  )
)

document_counts <- sentences |>
  mutate(
    source_group = if_else(
      document_id == "F001",
      "training flyer",
      "job-detail rows"
    )
  ) |>
  count(source_group, name = "rows")

first_sentence <- sentences$text[1]
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  document_counts,
  col.names = c("Source group", "Rows"),
  caption = "The 28 labeled text units by source",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(nrow(sentences), 28L),
  identical(
    document_counts$rows[document_counts$source_group == "training flyer"],
    6L
  ),
  identical(
    document_counts$rows[document_counts$source_group == "job-detail rows"],
    22L
  ),
  identical(
    first_sentence,
    "Paid 12-week training is provided."
  )
)
```

The first sentence fits on one line: `Paid 12-week training is provided.` A
**token** is one piece of text produced by a splitting rule. The same visible
sentence can produce different tokens because the rule makes different choices.

## Split on spaces

One simple rule is to split wherever there is whitespace. Here stringr uses the
ICU text library to find spaces, tabs, and similar separators. That rule gives
five pieces. The period stays attached to `provided.`, and `12-week` stays in
one piece.

```{r}
whitespace_tokens <- str_split(
  first_sentence,
  "\\s+",
  simplify = FALSE
)[[1]]
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  tibble(
    token_number = seq_along(whitespace_tokens),
    token = whitespace_tokens
  ),
  col.names = c("Token number", "Whitespace token"),
  caption = "Tokens made by splitting on whitespace",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(length(whitespace_tokens), 5L),
  identical(
    whitespace_tokens,
    c("Paid", "12-week", "training", "is", "provided.")
  )
)
```

This rule is easy to explain, but it keeps punctuation and hyphenated material
attached to nearby letters. That may or may not fit the count the Lab wants.

## Use a word tokenizer

`tokenizers::tokenize_words()` applies a different rule. It lowercases text,
drops punctuation, and splits the hyphenated phrase. The same sentence becomes
six tokens: `paid`, `12`, `week`, `training`, `is`, and `provided`.

```{r}
default_word_tokens <- tokenize_words(first_sentence)[[1]]
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  tibble(
    token_number = seq_along(default_word_tokens),
    token = default_word_tokens
  ),
  col.names = c("Token number", "Default word token"),
  caption = "Tokens from tokenizers::tokenize_words()",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(length(default_word_tokens), 6L),
  identical(
    default_word_tokens,
    c("paid", "12", "week", "training", "is", "provided")
  )
)
```

That rule is useful when `Paid` and `paid` should count together. It is a poor
fit if the Lab needs to keep punctuation as its own evidence.

## Keep case and punctuation visible

The function can retain case and punctuation.
With those settings, `Paid` stays capitalized.
The hyphen and full stop each become separate tokens.
The sentence becomes eight tokens.

```{r}
case_punctuation_tokens <- tokenize_words(
  first_sentence,
  lowercase = FALSE,
  strip_punct = FALSE
)[[1]]

token_count_summary <- tibble(
  rule = c(
    "split on whitespace",
    "default word tokenizer",
    "keep case and punctuation"
  ),
  tokens = c(
    length(whitespace_tokens),
    length(default_word_tokens),
    length(case_punctuation_tokens)
  )
)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  token_count_summary,
  col.names = c("Rule", "Tokens from the first sentence"),
  caption = "One sentence under three tokenization rules",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(length(case_punctuation_tokens), 8L),
  identical(
    case_punctuation_tokens,
    c("Paid", "12", "-", "week", "training", "is", "provided", ".")
  )
)
```

Five, six, and eight are all correct counts under their respective rules.
The count alone does not show the rule.

## Compare sentence splits before word counts

The file stores one text unit per row.
The Lab compares sentence-tokenization output with those 28 pieces.
Other files may contain several sentences per row or divide one sentence
across rows.

```{r}
sentence_pieces <- tokenize_sentences(sentences$text)
sentence_piece_counts <- map_int(sentence_pieces, length)
source_sentence_counts <- sentences |>
  mutate(sentence_pieces = sentence_piece_counts) |>
  summarise(
    rows = n(),
    pieces = sum(sentence_pieces),
    .by = document_id
  )
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  source_sentence_counts,
  col.names = c("Document ID", "Rows", "Sentence pieces"),
  caption = "Sentence tokenizer results by document",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(sentence_piece_counts, rep(1L, 28L)),
  identical(sum(source_sentence_counts$pieces), 28L)
)
```

For these rows, `tokenizers::tokenize_sentences()` returns one piece per row.
The file and tokenizer therefore agree on unit boundaries in this teaching
dataset. This agreement does not make every unit a grammatical sentence.

## Train a subword tokenizer

Modern language models often split text into **subwords**.
These pieces can be smaller than words but larger than single letters for
patterns learned during training. **Byte pair encoding (BPE)** starts from
single characters. At each step, it merges the most frequent pair.
The following model trains only on the 28 Riverton text units.

The `vocab_size = 250L` argument controls how many pieces the trainer can keep.
The `coverage = 1` argument retains every character in the training text.
Characters outside that set have no piece. The marker `<UNK>`, short for
"unknown", records an input without a vocabulary piece.
The setting `threads = 1L` removes variation from work division across
processors.

::: {.callout-note}
The explicit `model_path` sends the model to a temporary file during rendering.
:::

```{r}
corpus_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".txt")
write_lines(sentences$text, corpus_file)

bpe_model <- bpe(
  corpus_file,
  model_path = tempfile(fileext = ".bpe"),
  vocab_size = 250L,
  coverage = 1,
  threads = 1L
)

first_vocabulary_rows <- bpe_model$vocabulary |>
  slice_head(n = 10)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  first_vocabulary_rows,
  col.names = c("ID", "Subword"),
  caption = "The first rows of the BPE vocabulary",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(nrow(bpe_model$vocabulary), 250L),
  identical(
    bpe_model$vocabulary$subword[1:6],
    c("<PAD>", "<UNK>", "<BOS>", "<EOS>", "▁", "e")
  )
)
```

The vocabulary has 250 entries. Four special markers precede the boundary
marker `▁` and single characters. The marker `▁` indicates the start of a
word-boundary subword.

## Compare familiar and unfamiliar text

When the BPE model encodes the first sentence, common pieces such as `training`,
`is`, and `provided.` stay together. The rarer `12-week` material fragments.

```{r}
first_sentence_subwords <- bpe_encode(
  bpe_model,
  x = "Paid 12-week training is provided.",
  type = "subwords"
)[[1]]

unseen_phrase_subwords <- bpe_encode(
  bpe_model,
  x = "unpredictability biotechnology",
  type = "subwords"
)[[1]]

subword_summary <- tibble(
  text = c(
    "Paid 12-week training is provided.",
    "unpredictability biotechnology"
  ),
  pieces = c(
    length(first_sentence_subwords),
    length(unseen_phrase_subwords)
  ),
  subwords = c(
    str_c(first_sentence_subwords, collapse = " | "),
    str_c(unseen_phrase_subwords, collapse = " | ")
  )
)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  subword_summary,
  col.names = c("Text", "Subword pieces", "Subwords"),
  caption = "BPE pieces for familiar and unfamiliar text",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(
    first_sentence_subwords,
    c(
      "▁Paid",
      "▁1",
      "2",
      "-",
      "w",
      "eek",
      "▁training",
      "▁is",
      "▁provided."
    )
  ),
  identical(length(first_sentence_subwords), 9L),
  identical(length(unseen_phrase_subwords), 21L)
)
```

The first sentence produces nine subword pieces.
The unseen phrase `unpredictability biotechnology` produces 21 pieces in this
teaching model. Larger released tokenizers use different training data,
vocabularies, normalizers, and unknown policies.
Measure their piece counts instead of inferring counts from this result.

This example does not establish that unfamiliar material always produces more
pieces. The next comparison demonstrates the limit.

## What actually decides the number of pieces

Training used 28 English lines in the Latin script.
The setting `coverage = 1` retained every character in that text.
A character outside that set has no piece, so the model uses `<UNK>`.

The comparison adds a Chinese phrase meaning "training course" and a Greek
word. Neither text appears in training. The code also uses `type = "ids"`
instead of `type = "subwords"`. IDs report the vocabulary entry for each piece.

```{r}
unknown_id <- bpe_model$vocabulary$id[
  bpe_model$vocabulary$subword == "<UNK>"
]

texts_to_encode <- c(
  familiar_sentence = "Paid 12-week training is provided.",
  unseen_english = "unpredictability biotechnology",
  unseen_chinese = "\u57F9\u8BAD\u8BFE\u7A0B",
  unseen_greek = "\u0393\u03BB\u03C9\u03C3\u03C3\u03B1"
)

piece_report <- tibble(
  example = names(texts_to_encode),
  text = unname(texts_to_encode),
  ids = map(
    unname(texts_to_encode),
    \(one_text) bpe_encode(bpe_model, x = one_text, type = "ids")[[1]]
  ),
  subwords = map(
    unname(texts_to_encode),
    \(one_text) bpe_encode(bpe_model, x = one_text, type = "subwords")[[1]]
  )
) |>
  mutate(
    characters = str_length(text),
    pieces = map_int(ids, length),
    unknown_pieces = map_int(
      ids,
      \(id_vector) sum(id_vector == unknown_id)
    ),
    shown_as_subwords = map_chr(
      subwords,
      \(piece_vector) str_c(piece_vector, collapse = " | ")
    ),
    display_text = case_when(
      example == "unseen_chinese" ~
        "<span lang=\"zh\">培训课程</span>",
      example == "unseen_greek" ~
        "<span lang=\"el\">Γλωσσα</span>",
      TRUE ~ text
    ),
    display_subwords = case_when(
      example == "unseen_chinese" ~ str_c(
        "<span lang=\"zh\">",
        shown_as_subwords,
        "</span>"
      ),
      example == "unseen_greek" ~ str_c(
        "<span lang=\"el\">",
        shown_as_subwords,
        "</span>"
      ),
      TRUE ~ shown_as_subwords
    )
  )
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  piece_report |>
    select(display_text, characters, pieces, unknown_pieces, display_subwords),
  col.names = c(
    "Text",
    "Characters",
    "Pieces",
    "Unknown pieces",
    "What the subword view shows"
  ),
  caption = "Piece counts and unknown pieces for four texts",
  row.names = FALSE,
  escape = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(unknown_id, 1L),
  identical(piece_report$pieces, c(9L, 21L, 2L, 2L)),
  identical(piece_report$unknown_pieces, c(0L, 0L, 1L, 1L)),
  piece_report$pieces[3] < piece_report$pieces[1],
  identical(
    piece_report$shown_as_subwords[3],
    str_c("\u2581 | ", texts_to_encode[["unseen_chinese"]])
  ),
  str_detect(piece_report$display_text[3], fixed("lang=\"zh\"")),
  str_detect(piece_report$display_text[4], fixed("lang=\"el\"")),
  str_detect(piece_report$display_subwords[3], fixed("lang=\"zh\"")),
  str_detect(piece_report$display_subwords[4], fixed("lang=\"el\""))
)
```

The unfamiliar Chinese phrase produces two pieces.
The familiar English sentence produces nine.
The model learned nothing about Chinese.
One of the Chinese phrase's pieces is `<UNK>`, which records the missing
representation.

Piece counts depend on the tokenizer, vocabulary, script, language, and
normalization. The policy for unknown characters is especially important.
This model can represent unfamiliar text with fewer pieces than familiar text.
Replacing unknown text with `<UNK>` reduces piece counts but loses information.

The `shown_as_subwords` column displays Chinese characters without corresponding
vocabulary entries. The subword view reconstructs surface text instead of
reporting vocabulary entries. Count unknowns from the IDs, not the printed
pieces.

### Compare decoded text with the input

If a tokenizer cannot reconstruct its input, it loses information.
Decoding the IDs permits a direct reconstruction check.

```{r}
round_trip <- piece_report |>
  mutate(
    decoded = map_chr(
      ids,
      \(id_vector) bpe_decode(bpe_model, id_vector)[[1]]
    ),
    recovers_input = decoded == text
  )
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  round_trip |>
    select(display_text, pieces, unknown_pieces, decoded, recovers_input),
  col.names = c(
    "Text",
    "Pieces",
    "Unknown pieces",
    "Decoded from ids",
    "Recovers the input"
  ),
  caption = "Round-trip results for the four texts",
  row.names = FALSE,
  escape = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(
    round_trip$recovers_input,
    c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, FALSE)
  ),
  all(str_detect(
    round_trip$decoded[!round_trip$recovers_input],
    fixed("<UNK>")
  )),
  identical(
    round_trip$recovers_input,
    round_trip$unknown_pieces == 0L
  )
)
```

Decoding recovers both Latin-script texts exactly, with their punctuation and
digits. It replaces both unseen-script texts with `<UNK>`.
Only texts with unknown pieces fail this round-trip check.

Round-trip recovery provides a check of reversible text identity, not source alignment.
Some tokenizers return original-input offsets even when an unknown ID cannot
decode to its text. Tasks that mark spans or highlight matches need separate
checks of those offset mappings.

A word count must identify its tokenization rule.
A piece count must identify its vocabulary, script coverage, and treatment of
other characters.

## What to remember

- Tokenization produces text pieces according to a chosen rule.
- The first Riverton sentence becomes 5, 6, or 8 word tokens under three rules.
- Sentence tokenization preserves the 28 rows in this file.
- This teaching BPE used larger pieces for some training text.
  That pattern is not universal.
- Piece counts depend on the vocabulary, the script, the normalization the
  model applies, and its policy for unknown characters.
- An unknown-piece policy can reduce piece counts for unfamiliar text while
  losing all its content.
- Count unknown pieces from the IDs.
- Compare the decoded text with the input.

The Lab must record its token rule before counting.
The rule gives the counting unit before any summary calculation.
